clue.text: See 11
Noel right bag according to tastelesss 'Gotcha' victim

indicators.note: arranged in poor taste, so the letters are put in a rough new order

explanation.surface: Someone named Noel is told his bag is a victim, according to a tasteless source.
explanation.walkthrough: The Argentine cruiser General Belgrano was sunk in the 1982 Falklands War, and the Sun greeted it with the notorious headline 'Gotcha'. The clue's 'tastelesss' is printed with a stray s.
explanation.definitionFit: The warship sunk by a British submarine was the subject of the tabloid's gloating front-page headline.

clue.text: Colleague cuts Blair & co, down to size

indicators.note: cutting something down to size shortens it, so the end of the word is chopped off
with 'cuts', says the long word is trimmed to a short stub

parts.note: before 1997 Tony Blair and his Labour colleagues were the Opposition in Parliament

explanation.surface: A colleague humbles Tony Blair and his team, cutting them down to size.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1990s Blair led Labour in opposition; OPPOSITION cut short leaves its first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Oppo is British informal slang for a partner or workmate, originally from the armed forces.

clue.text: For one political faction, it's sadly fatal getting a hard on

indicators.note: means the following letters are added on
something sadly done is badly done, so these letters are shuffled

parts.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A smutty joke about a fatal erection, dressed up as a remark on a political faction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' just attaches the last pieces; the phrase 'a hard on' is there for the innuendo.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatah is a Palestinian nationalist party, an example of a political grouping.

clue.text: One sucker who'd hardly welcome a stakeholder society

definitions.text: One sucker who'd hardly welcome a stakeholder society

parts.words: One sucker who'd hardly welcome a stakeholder society
parts.note: Blair's slogan 'the stakeholder society' is read as a world full of people holding wooden stakes, the bane of a blood-sucker

explanation.walkthrough: The 'stakeholder society' was a New Labour slogan of the mid-1990s; read literally it means people carrying stakes, which is bad news for a creature killed by a stake through the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: The undead creature of folklore drinks blood and is destroyed by a wooden stake.

clue.text: Awoman's resentment of a member's nasty snipe at loveless ambassador

indicators.note: here simply places one piece next to the other
a nasty version of the word is a mangled one, so its letters are rearranged
love is zero in tennis, the letter O, so being without love drops an O

parts.note: an envoy is a diplomatic representative such as an ambassador

explanation.surface: A man makes a nasty snipe at a heartless ambassador.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awoman's' is printed run together for 'A woman's'. The Freudian term is the definition; 'member' sets up the innuendo.
explanation.definitionFit: Freud's theory held that girls feel jealousy toward males for possessing the male organ.

clue.text: Watch part played endlessly by Di as far as Charles is concerned

indicators.note: beside, so the pieces are placed next to each other
without its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a role is the part an actor plays

parts.words: Di as far as Charles is concerned
parts.note: after their 1996 divorce Diana was Prince Charles's ex-wife

explanation.surface: A royal-marriage jibe: Diana playing her part endlessly, from Charles's point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a verb telling you to observe the royals, but it is the definition, a timepiece; Diana became Charles's former wife on their 1996 divorce.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolex is a famous Swiss brand of luxury wristwatch.

clue.text: 'Hi' from Prince Philip, left out and swallowing an E as a stimulant

indicators.note: taking in, so one letter goes inside the rest
the letters are put out of order, rearranged
the greeting's letters are taken away from what follows

parts.note: the two letters of the greeting as written
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, here just the letter

explanation.surface: Prince Philip's gruff greeting, with someone left out and taking an ecstasy tablet as a pick-me-up.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing H and I from PHILIP leaves PLIP, which 'out' rearranges to PPIL; with P before and L after, 'swallowing' then takes E inside after the first P.
explanation.definitionFit: A pep pill is a tablet of amphetamine or similar drug taken to boost energy.

clue.text: Shaft backward Dicky, the showbiz celeb

parts.note: a mine is a shaft sunk into the ground

indicators.note: read in reverse order, from back to front

parts.note: dicky is British slang for unwell or unsound, as in a dicky heart

explanation.surface: A sly dig: a showbiz star whose shaft is backward and dicky.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid spells the singer Liza Minnelli's name with one N, as the wordplay builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: Liza Minnelli, star of Cabaret, is a famous entertainer and celebrity.

clue.text: One that likes a good greasing has roving hand

definitions.text: One that likes a good greasing
definitions.meaning: first meaning: to grease someone's palm is to bribe them, so a palm wanting it shows greed for bribes
second meaning: a restless, wandering hand, one that itches to grab

explanation.walkthrough: The sense of greasing as bribery is the key: a palm that itches wants money pressed into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Having an itchy palm is an idiom for being avaricious and open to bribery.

clue.text: Whether it's just an environmental scare story, a matter of degree?

definitions.text: Whether it's just an environmental scare story, a matter of degree?

parts.words: Whether it's just an environmental scare story, a matter of degree?
parts.note: the whole clue describes the climate debate, with 'Whether' punning on weather and 'degree' meaning both extent and a unit of temperature

explanation.walkthrough: 'Whether' is there for its sound-alike, weather, and 'a matter of degree' is literally about rising temperatures as well as the question of how serious the threat is.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the rise in the Earth's average temperature, a phenomenon some sceptics dismiss as alarmism.

clue.text: Naff Sun taking interest in divorcee of no particular gender

indicators.note: holds the next letter within it
naff is British slang for tacky or poor, so the word is spoilt and rearranged

parts.note: I is the standard abbreviation for interest in finance
an ex is a former spouse

explanation.surface: A tacky tabloid takes an interest in a divorcee's story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' is the tabloid in the surface but here only fodder: rearranged to UNS, it takes I inside to give UNIS, and EX follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Unisex describes clothing or styles suitable for both sexes alike.

clue.text: A dose? Put gin on balls

indicators.note: with 'on', says one piece goes after the other
with 'Put', places the second piece onto the first

parts.note: a dose is slang for a venereal infection, as is clap
a gin is a snare, a trap for animals

explanation.surface: A cheeky barroom scene: someone catches a dose and puts gin on their balls.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin here is the hunting snare, and balls is the slang for nonsense rather than anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Claptrap is empty talk or nonsense, which British slang also calls balls.

clue.text: Definitely a nation of arseholes producing such relentless competition

indicators.note: a race of rats puts the creature ahead of the people

parts.note: THE is the definite article
a rat is a contemptible person, here in the singular for a race made of them
a race is a people or nation

explanation.surface: A bitter jibe that a whole country is full of arseholes, leading to cut-throat rivalry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Definitely' is a joke pointer to the definite article.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the exhausting, competitive struggle of working life.

clue.text: Hardly a dung heap, then, southern Iraq in Clinton's eyes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a place where flies are not to be found, read literally
second meaning: the area over which the US under Clinton banned Iraqi aircraft in the 1990s

explanation.walkthrough: A dung heap swarms with insects, so its opposite is read as a place free of flies; the real sense is the military exclusion zone imposed over Iraq after the Gulf War.
explanation.definitionFit: A military exclusion area where aircraft are forbidden to operate, enforced over southern Iraq.

clue.text: Neil gaffe ("F off') scuppered the party

indicators.note: a scuppered thing is wrecked, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the letter F, removed as 'off' says

explanation.surface: Neil Kinnock's gaffe, with a swear word, wrecked his party's chances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'F off' tells you to drop one F from NEIL GAFFE before rearranging the rest; the expletive is part of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine Gael is one of the main political parties in Ireland.

clue.text: Sort of sex practised by Brenda in a carriage

indicators.note: placed within the vehicle's letters

parts.note: a buggy is a light horse-drawn carriage
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A scurrilous suggestion about the Queen's activity in her carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the Queen 'Brenda'; ER stands for Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Buggery is anal intercourse, an old legal term for a sexual act.

clue.text: Tabloid hack — he's broadcast a load of balls about

indicators.note: scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the letters of he's without the apostrophe
bull is slang for nonsense

explanation.surface: A tabloid journalist who talks a load of rubbish on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Garry Bushell was a Sun TV critic and columnist; 'about' just rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Garry Bushell made his name as a columnist on the Sun newspaper, a classic tabloid journalist.

clue.text: Combine lay and bunk off around one — what could be cooler?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the next one
the two words are mixed together into one jumble
the letters go off, into a new arrangement

parts.note: A means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's ideal: combining lying about and skiving off, nothing could be cooler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooler' looks like praise but is slang for a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lubyanka in Moscow was the KGB headquarters and its notorious jail.

clue.text: Architecturally renowned place — Prince gets the sweats

indicators.note: means the second piece is added after the first

parts.note: ague is a fever with shivering and sweating

explanation.surface: A prince comes down with a fever.
explanation.definitionFit: The Czech capital is famed for its Gothic and Baroque buildings and bridges.

clue.text: Recent divorcee steeped in craft — an expert

indicators.note: soaked inside, so these letters go within the boat

parts.note: a punt is a flat-bottomed boat
Diana, Princess of Wales, divorced in 1996

explanation.surface: A recently divorced woman deep in craftwork turns out to be an expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' is a boat, not a skill.
explanation.definitionFit: A pundit is an authority who gives opinions, a learned commentator.

clue.text: Adrink before no good potential turkey

indicators.note: says the turkey's piece comes first

parts.note: an egg could hatch into a turkey

explanation.surface: A drink before an unpromising turkey dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adrink' is printed run together for 'A drink'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a rich festive beverage of eggs, milk and spirits.

clue.text: Give credit to a big loser

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to identify someone as responsible
second meaning: a Lloyd's of London ..., one of the investors who lost fortunes in the early 1990s

explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd's Names were the wealthy backers of the insurance market whose unlimited liability ruined many in the early 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lloyd's underwriting member is called this, and the verb also means to cite someone for an achievement.

clue.text: Brenda: one who likes a flutter?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, a sovereign
second meaning: a butterfly species, which flutters; the Queen also loves a bet on horses

explanation.walkthrough: A flutter is a small bet as well as a beat of wings, and the Queen's love of racing makes both apply.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign ruler, and also the name of a large orange North American butterfly.

clue.text: Get delirious etc about arse of very fanciable type

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go round the other piece
wildly confused, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the rump is the backside

explanation.surface: A leering remark about someone's backside driving onlookers delirious.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumpet is British slang for a sexually attractive person, or such people collectively.

clue.text: None backing Colonel North for president?

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word reads from end to start

parts.note: nil means none, nothing
Col is the military abbreviation for colonel
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: No one supports Oliver North, the Iran-Contra colonel, running for president.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver North was the US marine officer at the centre of the Iran-Contra scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham Lincoln was the sixteenth US head of state.
